analysis.one_liner: Requires upfront all-in pricing for hotels and tickets, bans hidden junk fees, and ends early-termination fees for internet and phone.
analysis.headline: The Junk Fee Prevention Act was introduced in December 2025 with one sponsor and three cosponsors, referred to two House committees, and has had no hearing or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets the fees Americans pay on top of advertised prices: resort and cleaning fees on short-term rentals, service fees on concert and event tickets, surprise charges on phone and internet bills, and early termination fees for canceling a service early. Companies in these markets would have to show the total price up front, keep that price from changing during checkout, and disclose refund policies and how many tickets exist for an event. The Federal Trade Commission and Federal Communications Commission would enforce the rules, state attorneys general could sue violators, and airlines would have to report quarterly to the Transportation Department how much money they collect from baggage, seat-selection, and cancellation fees — a disclosure requirement, not a ban.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who books a hotel or short-term rental, buys event tickets, or pays a phone, internet, or cable bill. They would see the full price before paying, get refunds including the fees, be told upfront when a promotional rate ends, and could cancel service without a penalty fee. Shoppers comparing prices across sites would be comparing real totals instead of teaser rates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers booking travel, tickets, phone and internet

how_it_helps.text: Providers of short-term lodging and ticket sellers must display the total price, including all mandatory fees, in every advertisement and at the first point of showing a price, and the price may not change during checkout.

The bill bans fees that are excessive or deceptive, defines a mandatory fee as any charge a consumer cannot reasonably avoid or would not expect to be included, and lets the FTC write rules covering fees beyond the industries named in the bill.

Ticket sellers must disclose at least 72 hours before a public sale how many tickets are available, so buyers can see how few seats are actually on sale; sellers that do not actually hold a ticket must say so and give a full refund if they cannot deliver it; and refunds must include all mandatory fees paid.

Phone, internet, cable, and mobile providers can no longer charge a fee for ending a service early, must credit or rebate unused days in a billing cycle after cancellation, and must show one clear aggregate price on bills and disclose when an introductory price ends and what the rate will be after it does.

The FTC and FCC would enforce the rules under their existing penalty authority, and state attorneys general could sue violators on behalf of their residents to obtain injunctions, restitution, and damages.

Air carriers must file quarterly reports with the Transportation Department stating exactly how much revenue they earn from ancillary fees such as checked baggage, seat selection, and changes or cancellations, with a comparison by carrier published on DOT's website.

analysis.who_pays: Ticketing companies, hotels and short-term rental platforms, phone and cable providers, and airlines bear compliance costs and give up fee revenue that is currently buried in checkout. Some small hosts and venues may face costs updating pricing systems and advertising. To the extent fees disappear, the money may be rebundled into headline prices — consumers see the true cost, which is the point, but a sticker price does not fall just because a fee is folded into it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ticketing, hotel, telecom, and airline companies

drawbacks.text: The 'excessive' fee standard is open-ended: the FTC and courts would judge whether a fee is 'reasonable and proportional to the cost of the good or service,' which gives regulators wide discretion and could produce years of litigation and inconsistent rulings across industries.

Upfront display does not make fees vanish; companies can fold mandatory fees into the headline price, so consumers see honest totals but the advertised sticker price may rise to match, with no guarantee of net savings.

Small lodging hosts and independent sellers must rework advertising and checkout systems to meet the disclosure requirements, a real cost even if the rule is sound, while the airline section only requires quarterly reporting of fee revenue and does not cap or ban any airline fee.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is honest: people would know what something costs before they commit, and common traps — fees added at the last step of checkout, penalty charges for canceling phone service, unavailable tickets sold in good faith — would be constrained or banned outright. The main honest objections are the vagueness of the 'excessive fee' standard, which puts a lot in the hands of FTC rulemaking and courts, and the fact that transparency rebundles prices rather than lowering them. On net, the consumer protection is real and the costs are ordinary compliance burdens, though the breadth of the FTC's discretion is a fair criticism.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 4, 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Transportation and Infrastructure committees, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Janelle Bynum introduced the Junk Fee Prevention Act in the House on December 4, 2025.

The bill was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and, in addition, to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, for consideration of the provisions falling under each committee's jurisdiction.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the action history after the referral.
Three House Democrats are listed as cosponsors in addition to the sponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ticketing, lodging, telecom, and airline companies keep collecting fees the bill would have required to be shown upfront or banned, because the bill has not advanced. Consumers keep paying checkout surprises until any version becomes law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fee-collecting companies; no change for consumers

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats are attached to the bill — one sponsor and three Democratic cosponsors — but no Republican has acted on it and no opposition is on the congressional record; the only barrier so far is inaction in committee.

industries.industry: Ticketing platforms and secondary resale markets
industries.note: Primary and resale sellers must show all-in prices, disclose how many tickets exist before a sale, warn buyers when they do not hold the ticket they are selling, and refund failures in full. This hits service-fee revenue and speculative-selling practices that are legal today.

Resort fees, cleaning fees, and similar mandatory charges must appear in the advertised price from the first click and cannot change at checkout. Platforms and hosts that market low nightly rates with fees added late lose that pricing tactic.

Early termination fees are banned, unused billing days must be credited, and bills and promotions must show a single aggregate price with the post-promotion rate disclosed. Providers that rely on teaser rates and equipment or regional surcharges lose those tools.

Airlines must report quarterly how much they earn from baggage, seat-selection, and change fees, with the totals published and compared by carrier. This is disclosure, not a cap — a real transparency loss for carriers but far lighter than the rules hitting ticketing, lodging, and telecom.

analysis.trajectory: A first-term consumer bill with a sponsor and three cosponsors, divided between two committees, is unlikely to get a hearing or markup in the 119th Congress unless a committee chair picks it up or it is folded into a larger package. Similar junk-fee proposals have drawn industry resistance and no floor action. Expect it to remain in committee; some of its aims overlap with FTC and FCC rulemaking already underway, which could proceed without Congress.
